applicable_when: The kernel launches 5,880 CTAs with XBLOCK=128, producing 2 full waves + a partial wave of 1,657 blocks on 132 SMs. The partial wave alone accounts for up to 33% of runtime waste. Additionally, each CTA does so little work (128 elements) that L1TEX latency (15.5 stall cycles per warp) cannot be hidden — only 47.8% occupancy is achieved vs 100% theoretical. The fix is to use @triton.autotune to explore larger XBLOCK values (512, 1024, 2048) that reduce the grid to a multiple of SM count, eliminating the partial wave, and increase num_warps so each SM has more warps in flight to hide memory latency. With XBLOCK=1024, grid=736 blocks → ~5.6 waves. With XBLOCK=2048, grid=368 → ~2.8 waves, near-perfect alignment.

applicable_when: This is a pure pointwise copy kernel (load from strided slice, store to different stride). With XBLOCK=128 each CTA processes only 128 elements, creating 5880 blocks across 132 SMs (~2.78 waves). The kernel is severely latency-bound: 71.3% of cycles have no eligible warp because each warp stalls ~15.5 cycles waiting for L1TEX loads. With only 16 registers/thread there is ample headroom to increase XBLOCK significantly. A larger XBLOCK means each thread processes more elements (more in-flight loads), which hides L1TEX latency through instruction-level parallelism. It also reduces the grid to fewer, larger blocks, eliminating the partial-wave tail overhead (33.3% of runtime). Autotuning across XBLOCK={512, 1024, 2048, 4096} with varying num_warps will find the sweet spot that maximizes memory throughput while keeping occupancy high.
